speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: FELICITATIONS UPON RETURN TO HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE DUE TO ILLNESS AND ATTENDANCE AT SILVER JUBILEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with your permission and the permission of hon. members of the house I should like on behalf of all of us, before the afternoon's proceedings begin, to say to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister how glad we are to see him again in his accustomed seat.

subtopic: FELICITATIONS UPON RETURN TO HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE DUE TO ILLNESS AND ATTENDANCE AT SILVER JUBILEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: FELICITATIONS UPON RETURN TO HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE DUE TO ILLNESS AND ATTENDANCE AT SILVER JUBILEE
speechtext:
I am sure I need not say to my right hon. friend how deeply we all regretted the illness which rendered unavoidable his absence from this house for so many weeks, nor with what degree of real satisfaction we received from time to time reports of the progress he was making towards recovery, which recovery in deepest sincerity we hope has been very real, and we trust will prove to be complete. We were particularly pleased that my right hon. friend's recovery was such as to make it possible for him to visit England, and to be present to represent Canada at the ceremonies in connection with the silver jubilee of King George; also to take part in conversations which he had while there with the members of the British government and the prime ministers of other parts of the British empire. Possibly at his convenience my right hon. friend may wish to give to the house a word or two respecting the ceremonies, and also, if he is free to do so, with respect to the conversa-

Greetings to Prime Minister
tions he has had on matters of concern to us all. That, however, will be a matter for himself to decide and for the convenient moment. At present I just wish to repeat that, irrespective of party, as a united House of Commons, we welcome him back to the place which he has occupied during the past five years. I know hon. members on his own side hope, and we of the opposition join very sincerely in that hope, that he may find himself, regardless of what the fortunes of political warfare may be, sufficiently well and strong to be able to continue in the leadership of his party for .many years to come.

subtopic: FELICITATIONS UPON RETURN TO HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE DUE TO ILLNESS AND ATTENDANCE AT SILVER JUBILEE

subtopic: FELICITATIONS UPON RETURN TO HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE DUE TO ILLNESS AND ATTENDANCE AT SILVER JUBILEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure that on this occasion all hon. members of the house can forget their political differences in order to extend a very hearty welcome to the Prime Minister on the occasion of his resuming his duties as leader of this house. I concur very heartily in the sentiments so ably expressed by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) not only in welcoming the Prime Minister back to his duties in the house, but also in that portion of his remarks expressing our appreciation of the manner in which the acting leader of the house conducted the business while the Prime Minister was away. Having that in mind, I trust that the Prime Minister will recognize that in the event of his not feeling as well as he might wish, he can safely leave the business of this house in the hands of the colleagues who surround him. May I express the hope that the Prime Minister's health will continue to improve and will soon be fully restored.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FELICITATIONS UPON RETURN TO HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE DUE TO ILLNESS AND ATTENDANCE AT SILVER JUBILEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult to express in words one's appreciation of the kindly sentiments voiced by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the hon. leader of the third party (Mr. Gardiner). But I do appreciate their kindly expressions, and I thank them and thank this house from the bottom of my heart. Shakespeare said that:
The evil that men do lives after them, the good is oft interred with their bones.
So let it be. Whether or not there is any thought of that in the mind of hon. gentlemen who spoke I know notl I said to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) that there was another saying "de mortuis nil nisi bonum"; possibly that also was in the minds of some who are not in this chamber but perhaps within sound of the voices of those who are in the chamber!
But I should like to say how grateful I have been for, first of all, the prayers of many people. I do not refer to those formal expressions of sympathy or those formal appeals that are made to the Godhead, but to the letters I received from remote parts of the country, from the multitudinous poor, which make one believe after all that the great solid sentiment of this country is a sound sentiment and that the people have a proper appreciation of their relations to the problems of the country. Then to those who are members	of this	house,	on bothsides, may I express my very sincere and deep sense of obligation for the kind terms in which they have expressed their interest in my well being and welfare. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) was particularly happy in the expressions of sympathy which he conveyed on behalf	of himself	and his	party,	and thesame might be said of the party opposite and to the extreme right. Then the flowers, the telegrams and messages from various parts of the	world made	one think that	after allit was	not a bad	thing to	be ill	if for a
moment it afforded people an opportunity to speak well of one who is still living! But I value most the expressions of goodwill which have been made this afternoon with such apparent sincerity. I know that some -and this has been expressed in the printed page-have felt that there was no reason why one should be ill because one should not have worked so hard. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to say that during the last five years I have seen no opportunity to slacken or lessen the efforts I was compelled to make from day to day in the discharge of what I

Greetings to Prime Minister
conceived to be my duty to the country. That I overdid it is, of course, a matter that is known to most hon. members now; that I regret having overdone it is equally true, but if I had to do it over again I know of no way in which I might escape it, and I say that in all sincerity.
I am grateful for having had the opportunity to represent this country at the recent jubilee celebration, about which I shall make some further observations at another time. To the other matters referred to by the right hon. leader of the opposition, in connection with the discussions that took place in Great Britain between the prime ministers of the various overseas dominions and the Prime Minister and ministers of the motherland, I shall also refer later. It is sufficient for my purpose to say to this house this afternoon that the European situation is one of great difficulty, and at times it gives evidence of being very dangerous. But I am hopeful that the efforts which have been made during all these years by the government of the United Kingdom to secure, shall I say, a collective security pact and peace with disarmament, may prevail. Great Britain has disarmed to the point of insecurity; at this moment she finds herself in a position of very great difficulty. I think that is not too strong a statement to make in view of the knowledge we have all obtained from the press as well as from other sources. At this moment I shall not do more than say that I think it very desirable that I should at once make it clear that so far as this dominion is concerned no commitments were sought with respect to the matters to which reference has been made, nor were any given. I say that because it is desirable that there should be no false conceptions and no misstatements or misunderstandings abroad with respect to matters of such importance to us all. That the future is difficult to foresee goes without saying; that public men who have a firm and clear grasp of the situation are doing their utmost to preserve the world's peace is equally true, but that the task is difficult I do not for a moment deny.
A moment ago I was speaking of the health of the body politic. So far as my personal health is concerned, Mr. Speaker, I did consult the best opinions that I could secure, and the advice I have received is that if I were able to proceed with a certain amount of leisure and rest-I see one of my hon. friends who is a medical practitioner looking at me as though he knew what I was about to say, as he probably does-and avoid too much effort, in the fullness of time I might recover my wonted strength and health. I think I

should say to this chamber that they urged me not to return at this time, but knowing as I did what were the conditions with respect to this house and the date of its adjournment I felt it my duty to do so, whatever might be the consequences. I may not be able to give to public business that measure of attention and that strength of purpose that sometimes has characterized my conduct-so, at least, I have heard-but I shall do my very best while I am here to make clear what my appreciation of the situation may be with respect to the legislation that will engage the attention of the house during the balance of the session.
There are many things that men forget; there are some they always remember. When I say to you, my fellow members of this house, this afternoon that I shall never forget this moment, I but state the simple truth.

I think, Mr. Speaker, perhaps it would be better if I were to make a statement with respect to this matter because it has engaged my attention to some extent during my absence.
We have in this country a law respecting the dumping of merchandise, and we have also a law which has been on the statute books for many years with respect to depreciated currencies. I had no idea .that this question would 'be asked to-day, but my memory is that the provision with respect to depreciated currencies was passed .on the initiative of Mr. Fielding, the then Minister of Finance:. These provisions of our la,w apply to all countries that have depreciated currencies.
It is well known, of course, that for some time the currency of Japan has been depreciated and that the yen has not .been worth anything like its normal figure. The result was that automatically the provisions of our statute applied.
The re has been, it is alleged, an increase in the cost of living in Japan during the last few months with the result that the benefits that accrued under their depreciated currency did not accrue to the same extent to exporters from that empire to Canada. The matter has received the very careful consideration of an inter-departmental committee that was set up some weeks ago and they have been endeavouring to devise' ways and means whereby there might be such modifications of the provisions of the statute arising out of changed costs of living conditions as would be applicable to all countries, based upon the1 index of the cost of living as supplied by the League .of Nations. The. matter is still under advisement and my information this morning was that oommuncations had been sent to the government of Japan to ascertain the extent to which the changed economic conditions bad increased the cost of living index during the last few weeks, and to ascertain also what the report of the League of Nations' economic bureau was upon that point.
The matter is one of very great importance not only to the Dominion of Canada with respect to its relations with Japan but with respect to its relations with other countries whose currencies may be depreciated, for it is perfectly clear that if a currency is depreciated fifty per cent, then of course the basis upon which the tariff was arranged originally would no longer have the same application at all because a twenty-five per cent tariff, for instance, based upon the normal value of the currency of a country, would be only a twelve-and-a-half per cent tariff if that currency were depreciated fifty per cent, and that of course would mean disaster to many Canadian enterprises. All these factors are being carefuly considered, and from the reports which I received this morning I believe that a most earnest effort is being made to arrive at an adjustment that will be satisfactory; by that I mean an adjustment that will be fair and just to Canadian enterprise while at the same time not being unfair or unjust to trade between Japan and Canada.

speechtext:
I regret exceedingly that I was absent when the committee had under discussion this item with regard to the construction of a tunnel at the west entrance to the city of Toronto. I suggest that it would have been fair for the gentlemen who inaugurated the tunnel scheme to have taken into their confidence the people's representatives in this house and give them more information than they have offered in regard to this item. I may say that the city council of Toronto was unaware that this item was coming up for discussion in the house, and I will show later on that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Matthews) and the hon. member for
Public Works Program

Parkdale (Mr. Spence) were under a misapprehension when they said that the corporation of Toronto undertook to expend a certain sum of money to maintain the tunnel. I should like to make it abundantly clear that the members on this side of the house who opposed the item did not oppose any expenditure for the relief of unemployment so far as Toronto is concerned. I think the member for West Lambton (Mr. Gray) made it clear that we on this side are ready to expend any amount-the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) suggested $2,000,-000-to relieve unemployment. But the question was whether the expenditure was justified under present conditions if the purpose was to allocate it to the construction of a tunnel at the western entrance.
I need not urge on this house the position of the men and women who live on the islands of Toronto. They have an opportunity of getting away from the turmoil of the city, from all the traffic, from the noise and the smoke, in order to spend a few months on the Toronto islands. Now this may be a narrow way of looking at the matter. I am willing also to concede that at some future time there may be need of connecting the islands with the Toronto mainland in order to afford an opportunity to more people to patronize the islands. But the question that ought to be discussed at the present time is this: Are we justified in spending $1,000,000 for the construction of a tunnel, or should we spend this money in the construction of some more useful public work? Let me make it clear that the construction of the tunnel is not primarily for the purpose of connecting the islands with the mainland; primarily it is an airport scheme, and the tunnel is not required unless first of all an airport is established at the location indicated on the plan. I realize the need of airports and air bases, but the question arises whether this is the proper time to spend money on airports.
In the expenditure of public money I think we should adopt the same attitude as any individual who is spending his own private funds. We are passing though very difficult days of depression and it is about time that this government realized that public money should be expended only for useful purposes, because after all it is the taxpayers who will have to pay the money. I think there are many other useful works in Toronto to which this money could be allocated. For instance, there is the elimination of level crossings- something that endangers human life; these crossings have taken a heavy toll. Why not allocate this $1,000,000 to the elimination of eome level grade crossings in or about

Toronto? Then there is the question of slum clearance. The Lieutenant Governor of Ontario has handed in a useful report on slum clearance. The city council has not taken action in the matter-perhaps there are financial reasons

and there is an opportunity here for the government of Canada to help to put into effect the recommendations contained in Lieutenant Governor Bruce's report, by spending this money, and more perhaps, for the purpose of slum clearance. Then there is the question of building a court house in Toronto. The courts are now located in the city hall and the building is overcrowded. Here lies an opportunity of reviving construction-and nothing will get us out of the depression unless the construction industries revive. There are masons, carpenters and all kinds of builders, mechanics and labourers out of work, and the construction of a city hall would give them employment. I suggest that $1,000,000 used for any of these purposes would go a longer way than it would in the construction of a tunnel to be used only for an airport base.
I want to make it clear that in the plans prepared by the engineers of the harbour board of Toronto there is provision for the expenditure of $1,000,000 for the construction of a tunnel; but that is predicated, first upon the corporation of the city of Toronto expending $119,000 in connection with the tunnel; secondly, the sum of $305,000 in connection with the establishment of an airport; and thirdly, the sum of $186,000 in filling in lagoons and making parking areas.
The Minister of National Revenue in the discussion in the house at the adjournment made the statement that the city had undertaken to assume the cost of maintenance, including paving and ventilation, reducing the cost to the federal government to approximately $1,000,000; and the hon. member for Parkdale made a similar statement, that the tunnel would cost only $1,000,000 and that it would be there forever, maintained by the city. I may inform the house to-day that the city council has not been consulted about this scheme. The city council of Toronto has not agreed to maintain this tunnel nor to expend any money. It does seem to me that it is putting the cart before the horse. The harbour board might have approached the city council and obtained their opinion with reference to this expenditure, because as a matter of fact there is a great difference of opinion in the council. There are members of the city council who are absolutely opposed to the expenditure of money, not because they are opposed to spending money

Public Works Program
for relief but because they feel, as members of the city council, that there are many other purposes for which the money could be spent.
I need not take up the time of the house giving any further explanation of this matter. Members on this side are ready and willing to vote any sum of money for the purpose of relieving unemployment, but they feel that any work recommended for the expenditure of money ought to be, in the first place, an essential work; that secondly it ought to be useful work; and thirdly that there are more useful works on which this money could be spent. I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for North York (Mr. Mulock):
That the words "tunnel at western- entrance, Toronto" be struck out and the following substituted: "for construction of such public works or undertakings to relieve unemployment as may be agreed upon between the corporation of the city of Toronto and the government of Canada-$1,000,000."

speechtext:
There was never a vote
before this committee that was so much misunderstood and concerning which some of the speakers had so little knowledge of the facts as this vote of the 17th of April. The city of Toronto is the largest tax-paying city in the dominion, in excise, customs, postal receipts and other forms of revenue. It was said here the other day that the total was 867,000,000. You will find from the report of the Minister of National Revenue that customs duties amounted to 861,000,000, and postal receipts to nearly 87,000,000. The city of Toronto gets little or nothing. Comparison has been made of the Toronto harbour commission with the harbour commissions in Montreal, Quebec, Saint John, Halifax, Port Arthur and Vancouver, but there is no comparison. The other harbours I have mentioned are federal ports, money spent on those ports is spent by the government of Canada. In the case of Toronto it is totally different, the harbour commission is a city commisison, it spends nothing but city money. Any money that this government furnishes in connection with the entrances to Toronto harbour comes under the agreement of 1913, and is spent under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works. The Toronto harbour commission consists of five members, of whom three are appointed by the city-1
was a member for twenty-two years and chairman for some time-and the other two by this government. We never had any politics on the commission while I was there. There is in fact so little politics that while all the other harbour boards from Vancouver to Halifax resigned or were removed when a new government came in, this commisison has two of its members on it yet, two representatives appointed by the late government, they were on the commission in 1930 and are there to-day. They are two, good reputable men and they have done good work.
This proposition has been misunderstood. In the first place Toronto island is a breakwater in itself. It is formed by a sand bar, about three and a half miles long, and there is an entrance to the harbour at each end. Those two entrances are navigable waters and as such come under the British North America Act, and also under an act known as the Navigable Waters' Protection Act. By the British North America Act the government of Canada has jurisdiction over boundary waterways, interprovincial streams, and in relation to navigation. That is how it comes that the federal government has something to do with Toronto island. From 1867 to the present time the government of Canada have had to spend large sums of money for protection of the shore of Toronto island. Since confederation there have been some twenty-one votes, as shown in a return I had to an order of the house a few years ago. The government of Canada have always been responsible for that work, firstly under the British North America Act and secondly by the special agreement of 1913. In 1913 under an order in council validated by act of parliament a contract was made between three parties, the city, the harbour commission and the government. Any party to this contract who is aggrieved can bring the government of Canada into the exchequer court. We had the opinion of the law officers of the crown that there was a contract and we were about to bring the government on the viaduct case into the exchequer court when a meeting was held upstairs with the late Minister of Railways, the Right Hon. Geo. P. Graham, and we settled the case. So the contract has been established. The contract provided for some way of getting across these two entrances, the western entrance which is just east of the exhibition grounds, and the eastern entrance. The government of Canada agreed to build two bridges across those two entrances costing 8400,000 each. That was agreed in 1913 with the Hon. Mr. Rogers, then Minister of Public Works. This contract was signed and the three parties started work simultaneously;
Public Works Program

the harbour commission started its work, the city started its work and the dominion government started its work of building a turning basin in the industrial area at the east end and improvements to the western entrance.
Toronto island is a great asset to the city. But to-day very few people use the island. Hanlan's point is at the western entrance, where Ned Hanlan who held the rowing championship of the world lived. As I say, the island is only used by a very small percentage of the people. It can only be reached by a ferry boat. The ferries were privately owned until 1928 when the city took them over and they are now operated by the Toronto transportation commission. Instead of being used for only three or four months of the year by a small number of people this island could be used all the year round. It should be for all the people all the time, not for some of the people some of the time. The working people of Toronto carried the harbour by-law for the new harbour in 1911. In 1910 I moved in the board of control for a committee of the council to report on a greater harbour. The committee sat for nine months, and after investigation of harbours the world over we presented our report, which went to the people, and they by a vote of almost ten to one carried the by-law for a greater harbour. Fifty per cent of the work was a beautification scheme and the other part an industrial development, bringing into being a large industrial area in what is known as Ashbridge's bay where 760 acres of land have been reclaimed.
That work has gone on from 1913 until today, the work being now practically complete except these two bridges, one across the western entrance and the other across the eastern. Since these bridges were planned the traffic of the harbour has grown so rapidly that the type of bridge required instead of costing $400,000 would require $800,000. But the fact is that with the great increase in shipping, passenger boats as well as freight, the proposed bridges are now obsolete, as was found in the Detroit river, and a tunnel is considered the suitable provision for navigation and the safety of the public. It will be recalled what happened in the Detroit river, sometimes there were accidents with the ferries, and with bridges that would have to be lifted every few minutes there would be interference with shipping and with road traffic. Economy will be effected by substituting a tunnel for the bridge.
The expenditures of the city and the harbour commission amount to $28,600,000, that is entirely city money. The federal government has only given $8,000,000.

Bridges are out of the question in view of the increasing tonnage of the harbour. For example hundreds of thousands of tons of coal are coming in by water. Oil tankers come from all over the world bringing oil for Imperial Oil, British American Oil, MeColl-Frontenac and many other companies which have great areas of land and investments of millions of dollars in oil refining plants and storage facilities in the harbour area. The tonnage of the harbour has gone up from 959,234 tons in 1929 to 3,215,000 in 1934.
As I say, the proposed tunnel is the modem method of handling traffic under these circumstances. The estimated cost of the tunnel is given in the bill- at $1,000,000. Someone spoke of the maintenance of the tunnel as compared with bridges. If this bill passes an agreement will have to be made, fallowing the practice of 1913, to build the entrances. An agreement was also to be made between the city and the harbour board, and this government represented by the Minister of Public Works, providing for the matters referred to on April 17, by the hon. member for Toronto East Centre (Mr. Factor). These agreements as to approaches to and maintenance of the tunnel have not been completed, but negotiations are going on at the present time and it is hoped that in a few days these agreements will be concluded. The approaches to the* bridge of course, are a matter for the city, involving as they do roadways, road widening and many matters of that description*:
I may say that the city of Toronto has received very little from the federal government since confederation. We have not even a central post office there to-day; instead we have a number of sub post offices in rented quarters all over the city. We have been given a- few new buildings, but the large city of Toronto has not a proper, up-to-date post office. It was only recently that we were able .to get a customs house, though for nine ye*ars I salt in this house toying to get one. Toronto brings in. $61,000,000 a year in, customs revenue, but until recently there were only ramshackle buildings scattered all over the city. The city of Toronto is not asking for very much. Our case is similar to that of the city of M.ontreal, where the government contributed $14,000,000 or $15,000,000 towards the cost of constructing a bridge between the city and an island owned by the city. In Toronto the. new harbour plan and the new entrance are all provided for. When I was connected with it .there were no politics in connection with .the harbour board; previous governments have done very handsomely by the harbour board of Toronto.

Public Works Program
When I was sitting across the way we had a viaduct built there, and I give a great deal of crediilt to Right Hon. George P. Graham for the solution of that problem. The horn, member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) was also active in .the matter. When we started the greater harbour he was the pioneer who started that work.
The people want to use .this island all year. In Detroit they transformed .an island into a magnifioenit playground that is visited by people from all over the1 world, and the same thing could be done in Toronto. These islands cotuld be used all year, and if this tunnel is constructed a great deal of revenue will accrue.
Now I should like to say juisb a word as to the relief situation. The construction of this tunnel, as well as 'the construction of the airport and seaplane base, will mean a tremendous amount of work. I have an analysis here showing the percentage of the money that will be paid for labour. In connection with the tunnel the labour cost will amount to from 78 to 80 per cent of the total. In connection) with the subway the direct labour cost will amount to over 51 per cent and the indirect labour cost to more than 26 per cent, at total of nearly 78 per cent. In connection with the1 airport and seaplane' base the direct labour cost will amount to over 59 per .cent 'and the indirect, labour cost to more than 18 per cent, a total of almost 78 per cent. So you see there will be a great deal of work created. I think the time hase come when we must do more than carry on reconstruction and housing plans if we are to solve the labour problem and get people off the dole. We should be following the example of Italy, where the government are building in advance of the present age in oomneotian with municipal institutions of all kinds, such as hospitals, schools, trunk sewers, Labour improvements, registry offices and so on. All these are being built by the federal government of that country. It is far better to provide work for masons, bricklayers, carpenters and other skilled workmen than to have them on the dole. The Conservative party are protectionists, but if we believe in protection we should protect all the people; we should believe in it ,as a principle and not as a privilege for the eight or ten men who control the means .of production in this oountry to-day. That is where we all have gone wrong; we must bring protection up to date.
I believe that in this matter the Liberal-Conservative party is quite consistent, since 92582-183
nearly eighty per cent of this amount will be spent directly and indirectly for labour. All the newspapers of the city, including the Toronto Star, the Toronto Globe, the Evening Telegram and the Mail and Empire, have come out strongly in favour of this proposal. They think something is due the city of Toronto, in view of the revenues that have been collected there in the past and that are being collected at the present time. Toronto contributes well over $1,000,000 a week, and all we are asking for is $1,000,000 to help us with this work. I have a return here showing the amounts expended in various harbours, but I am not going to discuss that point today because I believe in the principle of confederation, each for all and all or each. I believe that what is for the benefit of Vancouver harbour is also for the benefit of Toronto harbour, Halifax harbour and all the other harbours, though the figures show that Toronto is receiving a very small return in proportion to its population and the revenues it contributes to the federal government.
There is a demand for this work from labour, as well as from nearly all of the municipal associations in the city. At the present time the island is used by only a few people; it has only about ten thousand permanent residents, who rent the ground at so much per foot and build their own improvements. If this vote goes through the island will be opened up to thousands of others. As hon. members know, because of the construction of the viaduct Toronto bay is only about sixty per cent as wide as it was formerly, and the result is that it has not the attraction it previously had. The city has taken over the ferry boats and invested a great deal of money in the island.
Reference has been made to the agreement of 1913. Let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, that Toronto is the only city in the Dominion of Canada that has contributed to the cost of grade separation. Toronto did not need to contribute one dollar to the cost of constructing the viaduct; the railways were responsible for that undertaking, but the city voluntarily contributed over $8,000,000 towards the cost of that work, though in other parts of the country grade crossings are eliminated under the grade crossing fund. Let us be fair to the city of Toronto and to the province of Ontario, which contributes about 44 per cent of the total cash taxes of the dominion but which gets very little in the way of public undertakings. The people voted on this proposition on January 1, 1911, and, as I have said, the by-law was carried by a very large majority. I do not believe I can add anything to that which I have

Public Works Program

' already said, except to repeat that the minister is to be commended upon the proposed expenditure. It will greatly improve the city of Toronto. We know that during the war that city was selected as the headquarters for operations of the royal air force. Eighteen thousand cadets were in training, and this number does not include the mechanics. Camps were located at Leaside, Armour Heights, Long Branch, the University, and at various other points. I say Toronto is the logical center for an air port, and that such a development would be in keeping with the general growth of the country.
Only a short time ago we celebrated the silver jubilee of the reign of His Majesty the King. If hon. members would look back twenty-five years they would bring to mind the beginning of the harbour improvements program, at which time the government committed itself to expeditures both by contract and under the provisions of the British North America Act., At that time the prediction was made that when automobile and air transportation were developed railway travel would be eliminated. That however has not proven to be so, because to-day the railway is still the safest and most economical method of transportation; perhaps it always will be. Today aeroplanes are used to a very limited extent as a means of travel; then, in addition in Europe they are used for the transportation of rich men, by frightened politicians who in Europe go from capital to capital, and by embezzlers who wish to leave the country quickly. But in Canada an important part will soon be played by commercial aviation. We believe however that the proposed expenditure will supplement expenditures being made by the municipality, and that commercial aviation may in time assume a proper relationship to travel by land and water.
I suggest it is essential that the proposed expenditure be made. While I must observe that harbour development originated through a Conservative administration, politics has not played a very great part in the discussion of plans for the Toronto harbour and the Liberals settled the viaduct case for us. In 1924 the city of Toronto approached the then government, and I believe upon this occasion I would do well to pay tribute to the then Minister of Railways, Mr. Graham, for the part he played at that time.
As the hon. member for Parkdale has said, we are not asking very much. Out of an expenditure involving many millions of dollars we are asking only SI,000,000, and I believe the government would do well to make this expenditure.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to support the appropriation for the tunnel to Toronto island. Before proceeding to make further observations, however, I should like to make some comments on the remarks of the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor) who I believe said that hon. members on his side of the house had not opposed the vote for the city of Toronto when, before the adjournment, the matter was under consideration. I would remind him that four hon. members sitting around him spoke in this connection and in each case opposed the expenditure.
First we heard the hon. member for West Lambton who, concluding his observations, said:
I think this committee as a whole believes that it would be to the better advantage of the city of Toronto if this amount of money weTe utilized for slum clearance instead of for the construction of this tunnel.
The question of slum clearance was not under discussion, nor does the bill refer to it. I would direct the attention of the hon. member to the fact that the bill referred to a tunnel, and that that was the matter under discussion. Then the hon. member for West Middlesex concluded his observations as follows:
But I think, Mr. Chairman, that this item ought to be cut out or stand until such time as the committee is given some satisfactory explanation in regard to it.
Again, concluding his remarks the hon. member for North Waterloo said:
Would it not be better for the balance of that $1,100,000 to be expended in the city of Toronto for other relief work which would provide the employment that this tunnel would give.
I say the tunnel is one item which will give employment. Whether or not under this vote the house would be prepared to discuss other means of providing employment, I do not know. I do say however that an expenditure for the building of a tunnel would provide employment, and I repeat that that is the subject now under discussion. Concluding his observations the hon. member for Melville said:
I do not think we should be asked to vote a million dollars to build a tunnel unless we know what it is for and how much it will really cost.
I suggest if the hon. member for Toronto West Centre had read the observations of hon. members on his side of the house-and perhaps he may have done so-he would have recognized that every speech made by his colleagues was made in opposition to the building of the tunnel.

Public Works Program
Now he rises in his seat and voices his opposition to this construction. He said that at some future time there may be good reason for connecting the island with the city of Toronto. I am one who believes the time has arrived when that should be carried out, and in view of the fact that 78 per cent of the money required for the tunnel's construction would be spent for direct and indirect labour I say this should be the proper time to do the work. That money would go into the pockets of workmen in cement mills and steel mills, and into the pockets of those men who in an indirect way, by their operations in factories, would supply material to do the work. Directly, money would go into the pockets of the men actually engaged in the operation. I can think of no item which has come before this house during the present session in which a greater percentage of the expenditure would go directly into the pockets of the working men.
Although I have not had time to digest the circular dealing with unemployment sent out by the hon. member for Temiscouata, I should like to commend him for his energy in compiling the details therein set forth. Upon casual consideration of these details one is amazed to learn the number of men unemployed simply because they have no trade and are in the class known as that of the labourer. In the building of a tunnel the ordinary labouring man would receive a great part of the expenditure, and I suggest that in this vote of a million dollars he would receive more than in any other items or other works of which one could think.
With no desire to criticize the hon. member, and merely by way of consideration of his observations, may I refer to the fact that the hon. member for Toronto West Centre stated that the scheme was one chiefly of developing the airport. As I see it the development of the airport is subsidiary to the building of the tunnel. In 1918 an agreement was entered into by the Toronto harbour commissioners and the federal government. Upon that occasion the then Minister of Public Works, the Hon. Robert Rogers, signed for the dominion. I believe at this point it will be proper to express my regret that the hon. member through illness has not been in his seat for some time, and I should like to state that the citizens of Toronto have a very warm spot in their hearts for him, and for the part he played in connection with the development of our harbour. I could present an argument for

the tunnel on the ground of the airport but the argument for the tunnel does not depend upon the airport scheme, although that is very necessary from the point of view of future development and additional reason for the tunnel.

The hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Church) has detailed the amounts that each one of the parties to the 1913 agreement has already contributed. There has not been any finding of fault with the city of Toronto for not carrying out its part of the agreement because, as the member for East Toronto has just said, the city of Toronto has carried out its part and has spent 64 per cent of all the money that has been spent under all these agreements.
It has always surprised me, Mr. Chairman, to see the anxiety of certain hon. members on the other side of the house, not all belonging to one party, to oppose votes for the city of Toronto. The background of such a member passes my comprehension, how he can rise and oppose just requests from that great city. The Conservative members, ten of the twelve members from the county of York sitting in this house, have never in my recollection risen and opposed votes for the great city of Montreal, for instance. That is a port that any country may well be proud of. It is one of the great ports of the world, and I for one would be delighted at any time to support any vote for Montreal harbour which the harbour commission felt was for the benefit of that great port. Neither do I recall any instance where the ten of the twelve members from York county sitting on this side of the house have opposed any votes for the great harbour of Vancouver, which is rapidly growing to be one of the great harbours on the west coast of North America. And, similarly, with respect to the great ports of Halifax and Saint John. I would be glad to support any vote that would be for the benefit and welfare of this country, and particularly if it is a vote that will provide a lot of employment and provide a large amount of labour proportionately, which this proposed tunnel will do.
Some hon. member-I forget just who it was-said that this tunnel would benefit only a small number of people. But, Mr. Chairman, I would point out that when these works are completed the number of people who will benefit from them will be tremendously increased over to-day. I for one very seldom

go to the island. When I want to go I have to go down in my car and park it in some parking ground, or else go down by street car, and after having done either one or the other,
I have to go into a pen and stay there perhaps ten or fifteen minutes, perhaps not quite that length of time, and then I have to rush over a dock to a boat, and on returning from the island I have to go through exactly the same procedure. The result is that only a very small fraction of the mothers and children who would dearly love to go over from the city of Toronto to the island, if there were only some way to avoid all this trouble and the payment of two fares, do go over to the island to-day. Toronto island is one of the finest breathing spaces on the continent of North America. I have travelled a great deal, have visited many cities and have seen their parks and islands, and I say this without fear of contradiction, that there is not a finer park anywhere on the continent of America than on Toronto island, and I for one am opposed to the few permanent inhabitants of Toronto island attempting to preserve that island for themselves, if they are behind any opposition to this scheme, and I do not say they are. The great mass of humanity, thousands and thousands of mothers and hundreds of thousands of children would dearly love to get over to the island on one fare, and to get there without having to travel over on a boat.
I quite realize that the plan proposed1 at the moment does not permit of their riding around the island or riding perhaps very far on it, but the hon. member for Toronto West Centre knows as well as I do that the Toronto harbour board has so laid out its plans that within a reasonable length of time-I believe they say three years more or less-what is called the lagoon will be filled in, and street car or motor car traffic will be allowed to go right on to the main part of the island. Knowing the hon. member for Toronto West Centre as I do, knowing his interest in the comfort and happiness of the women and children of Toronto, I know that he would like to see these thousands of mothers and children have easy access to the island, and I really cannot understand his opposition to this vote.

support it. The hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Church) referred to the amount of tonnage now entering Toronto harbour. As a citizen of Toronto I am proud of what the harbour board has done in this connection. The tonnage entering Toronto harbour is the third largest of any port in Canada, being exceeded only by Montreal and Vancouver. The Toronto harbour commission state that it would be practically impossible to build a bridge across the western entrance to the harbour. They state that if a bridge were built it would have to be lifted between six and seven thousand times during the season, so that taking everything into consideration a bridge is out of the question.
The hon. members from Toronto and the county of York

I shall not specify them- have at all times supported votes in favour of other large cities. As a member from Toronto I appeal to hon. members opposite to come forward and give our great city an opportunity to have every access to its island. This complete project will provide labour to the extent of over $1,000,000, taking into consideration the expenditures by the harbour board and by the government. The hon. member for East Toronto pointed out that Toronto furnishes twenty per cent of the revenue of Canada while Ontario furnishes forty-five per cent. I do not like to make comparisons with what other cities have received, but I would mention that last year and this year Montreal received over $9,000,000; Quebec received over $2,559,000; Halifax, $2,134,000; Saint John, $2,000,000 and Vancouver, $1254,000. If this vote is passed Toronto will have received, along with the votes of last year, a total of only $2,466,000. I do not think anyone can say that Toronto has been particularly favoured.
I cannot understand the attitude of hon. members opposite and particularly hon. members from Toronto or from the ridings adjacent thereto. I notice the hon. member for North York (Mr. Mulock) is ready to get up and support his hon. friend. He lives in Toronto and represents a riding adjacent thereto and I am surprised at his seconding the motion of the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor). I am surprised at his opposing the construction of a tunnel to the island.
The hon. member for Toronto West Centre referred to the elimination of grade crossings. I am in favour of such work as I believe there are some grade crossings in Toronto which should be eliminated. But the only question before us at the moment is the construction of a tunnel to the island and I contend that this vote will provide more labour than any other vote which has been passed recently by this
house. It will provide an easy access to the island and make possible a splendid airport for both sea and land planes. Of all the great cities on the continent of America, Toronto is the least favoured in this connection. Toronto is situated in the southerly portion of Ontario and is in close proximity to the great centres of population on the American side of the border. I feel quite confident that if we had an adequate airport there would be an increased air traffic betweeen Toronto and the great American cities.
There is a certain amount of opposition to a tunnel and the argument has been advanced that this matter came up in this house before being brought before the city council. I was glad to see the hon. member for Toronto West Centre at a meeting which was held in Toronto the other day. I will state quite frankly that the hon. member is as much interested in the city as I am. At that meeting the engineers of the Toronto harbour commission produced evidence to show that the procedure followed in this case was identical to that followed in every other case where the harbour board had applied to the government and there was no slight intended to the city council or any other civic body. If that is so I cannot see why there should be any opposition from the opposite side and particularly from hon. members from Toronto and adjacent ridings.

My hon. friend protests too much his desire to help Toronto in some way, in any way but that immediately at hand. I say frankly that I thoroughly agree that we would like all sorts of money spent on Toronto, I would like to see housing schemes, a new court house, any one of the things suggested, but hon. members who made those suggestions know as well as they know that they are sitting there that there is no hope of getting them at the present time, because those things have not been considered. I am interested in this because this work will be at the bottom end of the constituency which I represent and hope still to represent in this House of Commons. The people of that constituency are more interested than those in ridings to the right or left, but in common with all the people of Toronto they are interested in getting to this beauty spot across the bay.
What is the use of talking of allocating the amount of this vote to a housing scheme? Public Works Program

My hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott) said we had run along for twenty-two years without this tunnel. speechtext:
Yes, quoting it with
approval and adopting the language as your own, I take it. It is quite true that we have run along for twenty-two years, but the matter has become more urgent all the time. We might run along for another twenty-two year3, but this is the opportune and proper time to carry out the work. Why should there be delay when the money is offered to us by the government, to be spent in the city of Toronto? My hon. friend makes a point of the airport. I am quite willing to agree with him on that matter; I am quite willing to say that this will be of great advantage to the city of Toronto, inasmuch as it will connect the mainland and the city with the airport. That airport is an actual thing at the moment, although at present it is devoted only to seaplanes. Toronto must have its airport, and according to the best authorities this is the proper place for it.
For twenty-two years at least, to my knowledge, the idea has been held that there should be access to the island around the lake shore, both from the western and the eastern channel, and I say the time is opportune to provide that access. The dominion has made a solemn agreement to construct this undertaking, so why should we refuse the offer of the government, one party to the agreement, at this time?
I do not desire to repeat arguments that have been advanced already. Let me say in summing up that twenty-two years ago the dominion entered into a solemn bargain to construct this undertaking. We are still bound by that bargain, and now the dominion says it will implement the agreement and do its part. As I say, this is an opportune time, because we can spend from 8780,000 to $1,000,000 for direct labour in the city of Toronto. It is true that this tunnel will connect one part of the city of Toronto with the rest of the city, but this is a harbour. The city of Toronto could have operated its
little ferry boats across this gap had it chosen to do so, but the requirements of the harbour navigation prohibit anything of the kind. The harbour authorities knew that shipping would be interfered with if a fleet of small ferry boats should be operated; across that gap, and they decided that they could not operate the entrance properly with any such disturbance of navigation.
I need not go into the question of cost, because the tunnel will cost about the same as the bridge which the government agreed to construct. One point I should like to make, however, and which I urge upon members of this house, is that this undertaking is designed to help the common people of the city of Toronto reach a part of the city to which they are denied access at the present moment. This is the most beautiful part of the city, I think, during the summer months; it should be a playground for the people but now it is reserved for the few. Those of us who are anxious to see that the common people get all that can be given them are most anxious that this item should pass. It will not be money wasted; it will be money well spent, and for many reasons this is an opportune time to proceed with the work.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT

Mr. Chairman, as another Toronto member I want to apologize for rising, because I think perhaps enough has been said from this side of the house. I do not see why this item could not have been put through in five minutes, nor do I see why it should have been opposed as it has been by the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott). The hon. gentleman says he has supported many things for Toronto, but I never noticed that although I have watched his career ever since he has been in this house. The hon. member for Toronto South (Mr. Geary) has expressed my views and put forward many of the arguments I was going to put forward, so I need not repeat what he has said. The hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor), however, does not know what he is talking about when he makes the statement that the city council of Toronto are not behind this proposal. I have information to the contrary, and I think it will be found that the city council of Toronto are almost unanimous in their support. At the most I believe there is only one member against it, but one swallow does not make a summer. I must say that if other public men were as small as the hon. member for Toronto West Centre the city of Toronto to-day would not be much bigger than Newmarket or Aurora. I have
Public Works Program,

just had laid before me editorials from all the Toronto newspapers in support of this project. I do not want to read them; I do not want to take up the time.
I believe men who are elected by the people should have a vision of the future, but sometimes the vision exhibited in this house is not very great, even in connection with the development of a greater Canada. I remember that when I was a member of the city council of Toronto there were some public men who were very small, and I advanced the same argument then that I brought forward to-day, that if it depended on such people the city would not be bigger than Newmarket or Aurora. But that is not the class of men who build up. I have been behind every public development in Toronto since 1890, and particularly since I entered the city council in 1910. I was with my good friend from Toronto South on the first inspection made by the harbour board, in 1912, and I may say that the present consulting engineer of the harbour board is the gentleman who was chief engineer at that time. I believe he has made a splendid job of the Toronto harbour, and I think that harbour should be given credit by all Canada, and particularly by the province of Ontario, for the developments that have taken place. In Toronto harbour we have the third largest tonnage in Canada to-day. Montreal is first; Vancouver is next and Toronto is third, unless it happens that Saint John gets a few boatloads of wheat. I believe Toronto should be given some encouragement.
The agreements entered into in 1912 and 1913 between the harbour board, the city of Tononito and the government dealt with bridges. There was some diversity of opinion at that time, because we had people like the hon. member for Toronto West Centre, who had friends on the island who wanted to keep the island for themselves. The opposition to this tunnel comes from a very small minority, probably not more .than five per cent of the people of that city. One horn, member quoted me as having said that there would be no maintenance cost in oomneotion with a tunnel, while there would be in connection with a bridge. I did not say anything of the kind; I said the maintenance of a tunnel to the island would not cost nearly so much as the maintenance of a bridge. The tunnel will cost Sl.000.000 to construct, while the bridge will cost $800,000 or $900,000. The bridge will have to be of steel construction'; it will be an inconvenience all the time it is there, and after forty years it will have to be replaced. That is why Toronto has not been
fMr. Spence.]
agitating for the construction of a bridge. Many of us saw that it would be foolish to put a bridge there, because -of the' 'traffic through the western gap, which has greatly increased in the last few years. It must be remembered that the western gap has been dredged through solid nock to a depth of 27 feet; that is why our business has increased. The eastern gap cannot be dredged; it is sand bottom, which fills in again. The western gap always will be deep enough to accommodate any ships that come through the Welland canal.
I hope the members of this house will see to it that Toronto gets a fair deal. The exMinister of Public Works said this project would not provide .any labour, but I say he is wrong, and I think I know more about it than he does. I have been behind the construction of many bridges and hundreds of miles of roads, and I know how labour enters into the construction of these undertakings. This job will provide more labor in the city of Toronto than would be provided by any other job. There has been talk of a court house. Why should the dominon government build a court house .there? I believe we must have this airport, to keep pace with the cities of the United States. Take a trip to that country and see the beautiful airports they have established. We need this airport to provide another link in the chain of airports which it is proposed to build from Halifax to Vancouver. It must be remembered that at the present time seaplanes are travelling between the north country and the city of Toronto, and they must have accommodation where there is water. Why not bring the airport there too, and have them both together? The airport on Dufferin street is about six or seven miles from the centre of the city, and the one now suggested would be much more convenient. I fully realize that after the tunnel is built the city of Toronto will have to spend money, but the .maintenance charges will be nothing compared with the original cost of the work.
Aeroplanes now coming to Toronto do not land under favourable conditions, and particularly is that so when weather conditions are not favourable. I have never been in an aeroplane in my life; I have not enough nerve to ride in one, but I know that the conditions in Toronto should be improved. The proposed airport would be of a first class type; it would be up to date and probably one of the best on the continent. That is the way Toronto builds. Toronto spends money in development, and for that reason I suggest the vote now before us should have support.

Public Works Program
I hope hon. members. in the corner of the chamber, belonging to the third party, will see their way clear to lend their support. It ill behooves any hon. member-the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Gray), or any other hon. member-to rise in his place and knock any improvement for the city of Toronto. I would depend on the support of the hon. members of the third party rather than the support of the hon. member for West Lambton. It is ridiculous to observe how members from western Ontario knock the city of Toronto. I do not wish to read editorials, nor is it my desire to take up further time, but I do hope the house will delay no longer in the matter and will proceed to give Toronto the square deal it deserves.
As the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Church) has said, that city has spent millions of dollars on improvements, but it receives no encouragement. I shall not talk about what we receive, nor shall I go into detail about the money voted for the port of Montreal. I realize it is an ocean port, and I would add that hon. members have never heard representatives from Toronto kicking about expenditures made in Montreal. Further, we are not getting this million dollars for nothing; it is to be spent to give relief, and will not be wasted. We will be building for the future. More than seventy per cent of the money will be spent for labour.

I speak about the providing of employment and the manner in which it is being attended to in some parts of the country. I have before me a communication the contents of which I wish to place before hon. members. I realize that when a party is in opposition it is most virtuous-and I believe that observation would apply to all parties.

We are of the opposition. Upon several occasions the question of patronage has been discussed, and as a rule it has been raised by members of the opposition. From my seat this afternoon I again raise the question of patronage and direct the attention of hon. members to the manner in which work is being provided under the government's relief scheme.
I have before me a communication from the city of Calgary. This communication comes from the carpenters' union, one of the largest unions in the city of Calgary, and in it we find the complaint that in connection with the construction of the barracks in that city work is being given to men who are practically nominated through channels which ought not to have control of the providing of the work. I should be pleased to hand- the communication to the Minister of Public Works but I must observe that a statement should be made by the minister here and now to the effect that in giving work on these public undertakings no political interference is allowed.

I am sorry to say that I was not in the house upon that occasion. The communication before me comes from a responsible labour organization, and in it the complaint is made that a person has to have certain political credentials before his name is placed on the eligible list of those entitled to work. That condition should not obtain in any part of Canada. I do not know whether or not the Minister of Public Works is aware of such a condition, but I believe it is common knowledge that in .many quarters certain political influence is necessary before men are allowed to obtain work on the relief undertakings. That to my mind is one of the bad features of political life. A few years ago when the Conservative party were in opposition they claimed that men who wanted 
to get work on the Rideau canal relief works had to apply through certain officials of the party then in power before they could obtain work, and I remember the howl that came from the Conservative party. To-day of course the situation is reversed and there is no howl from the Conservative party in regard to providing work. I do hope that the Minister of Public Works from his place in this house will state definitely and most emphatically that so far as he and the government are concerned they will use every means in their power to prevent the unemployment situation being used as a political factor to provide work for the men who are unfortunately out of work at this time. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have no hesitation in discussing the subject that has been raised by my hon. friend. It is one of difficulty and one that has given the department a good deal of concern. The department does not desire that in the carrying out of these works there should be discrimination on any ground1 whatever. In some cases, as. my hon. friend knows, the work is carried out by contract and' the employment of the labour upon the work undertaken is to a large extent under the control of the contractor. I think my hon. friend will agree that the government cannot in a case of that kind dictate to the contractor whom he shall employ.

It is not the government that provides them. I do know that the contractors in some cases get lists from various sources. They get them from unemployment agencies, from churches, from returned soldier organizations, from Daughters of the Empire, and other bodies. The fact is that a contractor is simply swamped with applications for employment. The government leaves it largely to the contractor whom he shall employ, with this reservation, that we stipulate in our contracts that he must employ a reasonable quota of returned soldiers and local labour where it is available and competent. That is as far as we can go, I think, in reason with the contractor. If we go further, then the contractor has the right to make a claim for extras or anything else if you are going to dictate to him just whom he shall employ.
As to the work at Calgary that my hon. friend refers to specifically, that is under the control not of this department but of the

Public Works Program
Department of National Defence; but I do know that the government has no policy of discrimination and that it does not dictate or control in the matter of those who shall be employed on these works. It is not done through political channels, and it does not meet with the approval of the government if it is. But we do meet with this situation, that sometimes where friends of the opposition have been in control in a province, the complaint has been made that a Conservative cannot get work there at all, and these people come and argue that because they have been deprived of that work they should be given work by this government. We often get that complaint.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
We now have another complaint that only friends of another political party can get employment. Two wrongs do not make a right, and I do not think we can argue on that basis. I contend that any form

of political patronage in providing work to those who are unemployed is absolutely wrong and cannot possibly be defended by any hon. member. No matter where the works may be located, there should be no patronage in connection with the providing of work. The party in power, whether federally or provincially, is the only party which can put a stop to this practice. I have always been in favour of no patronage in connection with the granting of contracts and the providing of employment. I should like to read an extract from a communication received from the United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America, local union No. 1779, at Calgary. Alberta, as follows:
Contractors opened lists for the carpenters who had worked for them at various periods, and many workmen hoped that after waiting many months for the work to begin, at least they would be able to get a few days' employment. Now we are to understand that the only hope of ever getting work on the barracks job is when his name is on the approved list which is furnished to the contractors.
The minister has said that these lists might be furnished by the Daughters of the Empire, churches and other organizations, but he did not say that they might also be furnished by the political party in power. The communication continues:
The members of local 1779 request that when parliament is opened a protest be vigorously made against the practice of using this patronage list as it is debarring carpenters who are loyal and have been citizens of this country for the last twenty-five to thirty years, also a large percentage of the members being ex-service men. Owing to this approved list being used certain carpenters are being given employment by the various contractors on the scheme, thereby making it impossible for others to get employment.
I think that statement is fairly definite. It is quite true that this particular work does not come entirely within the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works but I assume that what applies in this instance will be applicable to other public works being undertaken by this country. I wish the minister would be explicit in answering this important question. I feel we are only aggravating a problem which has been a sore spot in the political life of this country for many years. It would appear that men who have lived in Calgary for twenty-five or thirty years, men who have served overseas, are being discriminated against because they happen to be members of a trade union and their names do not appear on an approved list. The minister was careful to make the statement that he objected strongly to such lists being given to contractors no matter

Public Works Program
from what source they came, but I wish he would be more explicit and state that he objected to lists being provided by any political party. I have no objection to semipublic organizations or churches providing contractors with lists of eligible members, but I do object strongly and always have objected to lists being provided by political parties.

I should
like to refer briefly to the point raised by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). I could not help but wonder while he was speaking whether the charge he makes was founded on knowledge or fact or simply upon the letter from which he quoted. There is a large number of unemployed in Winnipeg and I think my hon. friend is well informed as to the method that is adopted in placing men on the different works being constructed. At the present time there is approximately $3,000,000 worth of buildings under construction in Winnipeg, and so far as I know there is no system of political lists or political influence in connection with the employment of men. I have made it my business to keep in close touch with this matter because it so happens that the whole $3,000,000 is being expended in my constituency. I take no special credit for this as it happens that my constituency is situated in the heart of the city in which the works are being constructed. I am constantly in touch with it, and even if I did not seek to keep in touch with it there are sufficient unemployed to oblige me to do so.
The circumstances are these. The buildings are erected under contracts let by the government after public tenders have been invited and in each instance the contract is let to a
reputable firm submitting the lowest tender. The government exercises no control whatever as to who shall be employed on these works. When a contractor gets a contract for the work it is his responsibility to carry out the work in accordance with the plans and specifications and to a degree of workmanship which will pass the architect in charge of construction; apart from the supervision by the architect the government exercises no control whatever so far as the personnel of those employed is concerned, with this reservation, that in all contracts there is a specification to the effect that the contractor shall employ a reasonable quota of ex-service men. That is the only reservation.
With a view to seeing that that provision was carried out in spirit, I made it my business as soon as the works were undertaken to communicate at once with all ex-service men's organizations in greater Winnipeg, in order to obtain from them a list of needy unemployed ex-service men. I also asked them not to confine the list to membership in their organizations but to include all ex-service men who were in need of employment. These lists were made up by the organizations themselves from such sources as were available to them, and these names were supplied to the contractors. So that a contractor could not say, "I did not know whom to employ in the carrying out of that provision of the specifications." I can say this and say it very frankly and truthfully, that there was no question at all about the politics of returned men. If a man was an ex-service man in need of work he qualified. Thousands of names were submitted to me and I can say to the hon. member for North Winnipeg that no question was asked nor any information sought as to the politics of any man. These lists were placed with the contractors in order to put them in a position to carry out the spirit of the contract. Apart from that the contractors employed their own men and they are responsible for carrying out the works according to plans and specifications to pass the architect. They employ their own men. But with a view to seeing that those really in need of work obtained employment as far as possible, representations are made to the contractors from time to time by various organizations, by the federal representative on unemployment relief and by other agencies in the city of Winnipeg, all non-political. If the practice which has been indicated by the hon. member for North Winnipeg prevailed to any large extent at this time, surely it would come to our notice in the city of Winnipeg.
I say that it does not exist.

the .member for Toronto Northwest said: We have only this vote to consider, and we cannot consider any other; we cannot consider slum clearance, for that is not under debate. Mr. Chairman, this afternoon and again this evening I listened with a good deal of interest to the observations of hon. members opposite. I believe I could clarify the situation by directing attention to two or three points. First may I lay down the principle, one to which no hon. gentleman would take objection, that the development of a port such as the port of Toronto is one of national importance. That point was recognized long ago, and in order that the end might be achieved an agreement was made under the provisions of which the city of Toronto by itself or through its harbour commissioners was to undertake and complete certain works in Toronto harbour, and the Dominion of Canada was to contribute its share to this important national undertaking. The provisions were distinctly outlined, and the contribution which the city of Toronto and harbour commission were to make has been made. The contribution the Dominion of Canada was to make has been fulfilled only in part.
In this connection I believe it is necessary to refer only to that part of the undertaking in which the Dominion of Canada agreed to construct a bridge across the western entrance to Toronto harbour. At the time the agreement was made a bridge may have been sufficient, but conditions have changed. Public Works Program
is involved in the construction of a tunnel, the only difference being that had a bridge been constructed there would have been annua! maintenance charges.

Surely hon. members opposite do not contend that the port of Toronto should not be developed or that any agreement made respecting its development should not be observed. in cooperation with the provincial government, and with such assistance as may necessitate as a matter of general policy the passage of legislation by this chamber.

I submit there is no work there or elsewhere which will more literally or substantially comply with the avowed purpose and object of the measure now before us than this work, wdiich will provide an expenditure on labour of between seventy and eighty per cent. The object of the bill is the carrying out of useful works, works which will employ labour and give such employment immediately. I cannot think of any work which could be more readily undertaken or which would employ a larger volume of labour than would the construction of this tunnel. But no one knows yet
who it will be. That is still a secret of the gods, and that is why I strongly object. We do not know who is going to be responsible. Why is the legislation drafted the way it is?

It is just a bait for the electorate, so that the government can say to the people of Toronto, " We will build you a wonderful tunnel," when all that will be done will be simply to remove a small quantity of earth sufficient to bury the defeated Tory candidates. It is the same old story,
this government borrowing money all the time. It reminds me of the man who borrows $2,000 and wants to refund it, so he goes to another bank and borrows $3,000, and pays off the S2,000 that he owes; but still he is in debt and so he goes to another bank and borrows $5,000 and says to himself: I will pay off what I owe the other party. ment when he wishes, make an answer like that. Surely he is not serious when he suggests that the money will never be paid back. I ask the minister once more, under what department this tunnel construction will come. Next to him sits the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau). He is in charge of harbours. speechtext: I suggest to the hon. gentleman that if his services to his party were more valuable he would be a member of the cabinet representing the city of Toronto.
