This bill came up on one or two occasions before the house adjourned for the recess of five weeks. It is an important measure, the object being to vote $33,000,000 to be expended in this country, and we are asked to vote this money notwithstanding the fact that in June, 1934, this parliament voted $40,000,000 for unemployment purposes. If that $10,000,000 had all been spent I could understand why we should be asked to vote this $33,000,000; but we are told by the government that up to March of this year only $10,000,000 of the S40.000.000 had been spent. I notice to-day that the Minister of Public Works is getting busier. The nearer we get to the elections the more orders in council will be passed to try to hurry up contracts or the arrangements for the expenditure of the $40,000,000 voted last year. But in view of the fact that, in spite of the horse stables in Calgary and other expenditures contemplated in the bill last year, the government
Public Works Program

could spend only $10,000,000 in nine months, I see no reason why we should be called upon now to vote this large sum of money at the present time.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: An election is coming.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I know there is an election and I presume that is the reason. As I said a moment ago, this important bill providing for the expenditure of 333,000.000 came up in this house only about twenty-four hours before the adjournment on April 17, and this particular vote with regard to the Toronto tunnel was brought forward only at the eleventh hour and fifty-ninth minute before that adjournment. At that time very little was said with regard to the reason given tonight for this expenditure-that it is intended to provide an easy access to the airport on the island near the city of Toronto. On the former occasion before the adjournment we were told that the tunnel was necessary in order that the people of Toronto might be able to go to the playground on the island. To-day government members are changing their tactics and we are now informed that the reason for this expenditure of $1,000,000 is the fact that an airport is in course of construction or that it is proposed to construct an airport on this island.
I should like to know from the minister whether this airport is a private matter or a municipal matter, or whether it is proposed to be a federal expenditure. Does it come under the department of the Minister of National Defence? Is it to be built by the city authorities of Toronto or will it be built by private capital? We on this side have been blamed, we were blamed shortly after the adjournment on April 17, for blocking this bill and holding up the expenditure of the money provided for in it. I have under .my hand a dispatch from Ottawa sent out by one of the newspaper men in the gallery. It reads:
The blockade by which the Liberal opposition , in the Commons prevented the passage of the government's public works program before the adjournment for the long Easter recess is likely to cost Canadian workers in railway equipment shops several million dollars in loss of wages during the coming season, it is learned to-day in government circles.
I do not know how this gentleman got this information from government circles, but I may say to him or to anyone else who believes anything contained in this dispatch that the members of the Liberal opposition made it quite clear that they were perfectly willing to sit in parliament and discuss the matter,

being opposed to the adjournment. And I believe there were a great many members on the other side who were opposed to an adjournment of five weeks from April 17 to May 20. The great majority of the members of the house were opposed to it, and therefore no one has any right to criticize the Liberal opposition for delaying the passage of this bill. It was the government who wanted the adjournment. At half past five on April 17, when he found that there was some information required in regard to one or two of these items, the Minister of Finance moved that the committee rise and report progress. The Liberal members, and Conservative members as well, were willing to sit and have the bill and the schedule properly discussed, so that any moneys which the house deemed it necessary to vote in the interests of the unemployed should be passed upon before the house adjourned for that long Easter recess. I say therefore to the gentleman who wrote this dispatch, which was published all over the country, that it is not fair or decent to try to blame the Liberal opposition on the ground that the passage of the bill has been delayed. He goes on to say in this dispatch:
The program as originally drawn up contemplates the expenditure of $15,000,000, but the expectation of the government was that the legislation authorizing it would be passed without any delay and an immediate start made possible.
Does the writer of this article think that it would be fair to the taxpayers of this country for this house to pass in twenty-four hours a bill involving the expenditure of 333,000,000? Is it right or fair to the taxpayers of Canada that their representatives in parliament should be denied adequate time to discuss so important a matter? If anyone is to blame for delay in the passage of the bill it is not the Liberal opposition but the government, who wanted the adjournment for special reasons of their own.
With regard to the railway vote-and it is referred to in the dispatch-I think I voice the sentiments of the people at large when I say that as regards a vote for the railways, for the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, we are quite willing that, provided proper precautions are taken, the money indicated in the bill should be spent. But we object to an expenditure, whether in connection with railways or any other matter, which will mean that contractors will use steam shovels, as in connection with the Toronto tunnel, while little money will be spent for labour. With regard to the moneys

Public Works Program
for the railways, this gentleman is trying to make the railway people believe that the Liberal opposition is opposed to the votes of $9,000.000 and 88.000,000-

speechtext: I wish to say a word about this item, rather to clear my mind than to offer any criticisms. The minister has said that the Toronto harbour is of national importance., which statement I shall not deny, though there is no doubt that it is not of the same character as the harbour of Montreal or the harbour of Quebec. I understand that the Toronto harbour commission is not a federal body but is appointed by the city of Toronto. I understand further that the harbour of Toronto is the property of the city. What I want to know is, does the work of which that million dollars is to be spent become the property of the city of Toronto? When this government spends money in the harbours of Montreal or Quebec, that work remains a federal property under the harbour commission, and the responsibility is federal. But when the government spends money in the Toronto harbour, is that money a pure gift to the city of Toronto? I am not going so far as to object even to a gift, but I should like to have the difference made clear between spending 83,500,000 in Montreal on works that remain federal property under the harbour commission appointed by this government, and spending money on a tunnel in Toronto. Will the tunnel become the property of the city of Toronto? There is certainly an essential difference there. The minister says that Toronto harbour is of national importance, bu.t it has not in the past been treated as such because it is the city's property, while the national harbours are the property of the federal government under a federal commission. Will the minister >be good enough to explain the difference between the two situations, and clear ,my miind as to how the money is to foe spent and whether the works constructed are given- to Toronto or remain the property of the federal government?

speechtext:
The first point the minister made when he proposed this vote was that it was in fulfilment of an obligation incurred in 1913. That point was made also by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Matthews) when he was speaking as a member for Toronto. Since that time I think my hon. friends have realized how extremely weak that is as a ground for putting through this vote at this time, and we have seen some rather remarkable gyrations on the other side of the house. At one moment it wras said that it was for the benefit that would come to those who live on the island, then that there was to be an airport there. Now my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works is back to the original promise of 1913. He says that because twenty-two years ago the friends of my hon. friends then in power made a promise, we should now in 1935 when this country needs the money in the worst way take that as an excuse for spending a million dollars to build this tunnel in Toronto, as an emergency. And what does he say about it? He says that in 1913 we promised to build a bascule bridge. They have managed to get along without the bascule bridge up to the present time. I presume that bridge was going to be built in order to see to it that the ferries connecting the city with this island did not interfere with the traffic, but apparently traffic has managed to get along for these twenty-two years without the construction of

Public Works Program
the bridge, and without any extra means of communication. But now in 1935, on the eve of an election, this twenty-two year old promise is to be fulfilled. As my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Fraser) suggests, it is just like my hon. friends opposite; they begin to fulfil promises twenty-two years after they are made. They have made some more that I do not think will be fulfilled even in that time, judging by the magnitude of the promises they made in 1930.
I submit that there is nothing in the answer given by the Minister of Public Works. He has to have some other reason than this old, mouldy promise made in 1918. His friends were in power until 1921; they had eight years. His friends have been in power since 1930 and it is now 1935; that is five years more. Why did they not do it long ago if the carrying out of this promise was so important? Now when this country is having to borrow money and has gone into debt to the tune of over $800,000,000 in the five years during which my hon. friends have been in power, they propose to spend SI .000.000 in order to fulfil this promise. There must be some better reason than that. My hon. friend says it is for the purpose of providing employment. I agree that probably it will afford some employment, but as a first principle in connection with these public works the minister lays down that you must have a useful, productive, self liquidating public work. Those were his words. Secondly he says you must have works which will provide employment. I submit there is nothing in the fact that there was a promise made in 1913 which makes this a self liquidating public work. This is not the kind of work we are doing under the financial stress which exists to-day. and I submit that this house is not here for the purpose of paying the overdue promissory notes of the government which was in power in 1913 unless the public works which were then promised are of the class described by the minister.
Further than that the minister rather ridiculed the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Gray) when he suggested that this money should be used for slum clearance; the minister suggested that that was a provincial matter. The hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) brought out the point that this very tunnel is a purely municipal matter. In this case the minister says an airport is going to be constructed some day if somebody decides to spend the money,, but in the meantime the people of the Dominion of Canada are to
be taxed for $1,000,000 out of federal funds in order to build a tunnel across to that island in the hope and with the vague possibility that somebody may think it worth while to spend the money for an airport when the time comes. I suggest to my hon. friend that the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) was quite right the other day when he said that the bridge had not been built in 1913 because they could not make up their minds whether they wanted a bridge or a tunnel while others wanted nothing at all, and they apparently have not made up their minds yet. As my hon. friend! from West Lambton pointed out to-night, the Toronto authorities have not yet decided what they want in connection with this particular work. I submit that if my hon. friend is going to put this on the basis of an airport he should have some understanding first, some commitment from somebody, that an airport is going to be built. Otherwise what is the use of spending $1,009,000 and saying we are preparing for an airport without knowing whether there will ever be one? Before he has an airport he and the Minister of National Defence will have to have the plans for that airport; they will have to know whether it is feasible and whether it fits in with the national system of aviation.. My hon. friend knows perfectly well .that there is an airport at Lea-side now. I do not know whether or not it is sufficient, but no representations have been made by the Minister of National Defence, who has charge of aviation, that further accommodation is required in Toronto. So I say this vote cannot be justified by this old, forgotten promise, nor can. the minister justify it on the ground that it is for an airport when he has no commitment from anybody to build an airport. In addition, as my hon. friend from West Lambton has stated, I do not think the people of Toronto themselves are convinced as to the necessity for this work.

My hon. friend from

Until the authorities of Toronto are of one mind in connection with this matter, and until the Minister of Public Works has something to bring before this committee in the way of a work which will be a feeder to something which is going to be actually established, rather than something which is in the far distant future and is merely a matter of hope in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite, I have a suggestion to make in connection with a project of this kind which I think will much more nearly fill the bill and meet the requirements which the minister has laid down. The minister knows, or at least his officials know, that there is a community on Cape Sable island, consisting not of one hundred families or less as is the case with this island in Toronto harbour, but of about two thousand or more citizens, engaged in the fishing industry out there in the Atlantic. This is a focal point where men bring their fish, and from which they go out, where probably about $500,000 worth of fish are handled during the year. It is a distributing point for the Tusket islands and Seal island, out in the Atlantic. If my hon. friend wants to vote money to provide employment and also to provide a means of communeiation with the mainland, there is a place where he can do it with great benefit and justification there. This is a project which will be for the benefit of the community; he can make it self liquidating in the sense that it will produce revenue in the shape of increased catches of fish and increased facilities for the marketing of these fish. Here is an opportunity for him. My hon. friends may say this is a provincial project, but I say this very government and the government that preceded it recognized that these facilities were necessary. The previous government had already constructed two ice piers in the channel between. Barrington Passage and Cape Sable island with the idea that the provincial government some time might put a bridge there, and the government of my hon. friends actually constructed terminals for a ferry service, recognizing that these people needled facilities of that kind. You do not need anything like a million dollar tunnel down there, where you have two thousand industrious, hardworking, enterprising people who are bringing in new wealth every year. If you have a million dollars to spend, until the city of Toronto or the harbour commission or whatever authority is going to build this 
airport make up their minds and decide an airport is needed I suggest that you spend some of that money in providing decent facilities for communication between the mainland and Cape Sable island, where these enterprising people live. This is a project that I can recommend to my hon. friend without hesitation, and I would hope that the Minister of Finance would recommend it also. I think my proposal would be very much more in keeping with the principles under which money for relief works is being voted to do this than to proceed blindly, in the dark, simply because in 1913 somebody wrote into an order in council that they would build a bascule bridge, and now in 1935, just before an election, to vote $1,000,000 for a tunnel on the ground that the promise which we have disregarded for twenty-two years must suddenly be fulfilled.
I submit that there is nothing more than that behind this vote. My hon. friends wanted to spend $1,000,000 in Toronto; they wanted an excuse to do so and they found this old order in council. This matter of the airport has been simply dragged in in order to justify this expenditure, but my hon. friend knows there is really no commitment, no considered decision and no undertaking that this airport will ever be built. I commend the Cape Sable island-Barrington project to my hon. friend, and I say this committee can well afford to wait until we have more information before voting this million dollars in connection with this project about which there seems to be so much uncertainty and contradictory opinion.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the only question which the people of Toronto voted on in connection with the harbour was the question which was submitted to them in the form of a by-law in 1911: Are you in favour of a new harbour commission to have supervision over the whole fifteen miles of waterfront, with the members to be appointed by the city council? That by-law was carried and the new harbour commission appointed. Prior to that there was an old harbour commission which had jurisdiction only over the old Toronto bay, but the new harbour commission was given jurisdiction over the waterfront from the Humber river along the north shore, including Humber bay, the old Toronto bay and the whole territory east of the eastern gap as far as Woodbine avenue. The harbour commission's jurisdiction ran from the Humber river in the west to Woodbine avenue, and for a distance of three miles south. The people voted on that by-law for the appointment of a new commission: 18,460 yeas, and 4,720 nays.
The old western entrance to Toronto harbour was at a point which would be about three quarters of a mile inland to-day. A new entrance was made and built under the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. As I said this afternoon, both political parties have dealt fairly with the city of Toronto in connection with harbour improvements. We have had Liberals and Conservatives on the harbour commission and we all worked for the good of Toronto harbour. The new entrance was built in 1907 for $700,000. Mr. Pugsley happened to be Minister of Public Works at the time, and the work was very well done, the new entrance being two thousand feet long and four hundred feet wide,

with eighteen feet of water. There were just two parallel cribs; the north crib was all water and the south crib was all water. Seventy-five acres of water lots north and south of the western channel were dedicated by the Laurier government to the new harbour board, in a deed of trust, for park purposes, aquatic purposes, and a marginal way, and the commission filled in all that seventy-five acres. At one time Mr. Solman, who had a ball park over at Hanlan's Point, wanted to move his ball park to the city on account of the dilapidated ferry service to the island. I remember the harbour board and the private applicant Mr. Solman, who was a brother-inlaw of Edward Hanlan, meeting at the old Union station in connection with his application. Mr. Solman was a public spirited citizen; he had built the old rink on Mutual street and the Alexandra theatre, and he owned the ball park at the island. He went to the minister, Hon. Mr. Graham, who had always been very much interested in the harbour and in the baseball team, and applied for permission to use for a ball park five acres of that seventy-five acres that was originally dedicated for aquatic and park purposes and a marginal way. Permission was granted and the ball park was built on the north side of the new entrance. On the south side of the newr entrance there was a water lot, which has been filled in by the harbour commission. The sand for filling came out of the lake. They had a pipe line five or six thousand feet out in the lake, and they filled in all that land south of the west entrance and made it into a very valuable property.
With respect to the use of these lands on the south side for an airport, there will have to be another order in council passed along the lines of the order in council respecting the application for the ball park, to enable the harbour commission to use it for airport purposes. Toronto is a federal harbour, as hon. gentlemen may see if they look up the act of 1911. It is in a somewhat different position from Halifax and other harbours as regards the division of the work between the city and the government. The harbour board consists of five members, three appointed by the city, one by the government and one nominated by the Toronto board of trade which has taken a great interest in the harbour since 1854. Some of the old commissioners are still on the harbour board. There may be a difference of opinion as to the merits of this or any other scheme in connection with the Toronto harbour, but all the money that is spent by the Toronto harbour commission as a federal commission is

Public Works Pruymrn
purely city money, money handed to them by the board of control of the city, some of which is raised 'by city taxes. No Toronto harbour deficits have ever been paid by this government, and all the improvement of federal lands has been paid for by the city taxpayer. The harbour board bought the largest dredges in the world, one of which was the Cyclone, and filled up all these waterfront lots for twelve miles, including the industrial area in Ashbridge's bay.
The people of Toronto did not vote on bridges. They voted only on the question: Are you in favour of a reconstruction of the harbour and a new fusion harbour board. Under the Harbour Act of 1854 four bodies had something to say about Toronto harbour-the property department of the city, the provincial government, the federal government, and the old harbour board. There were thus four different bodies having a say in the harbour, and it is no wonder that Toronto harbour was away behind the times. When I became controller in 1910 I moved for the appointment of a committee to bring about a fusion board in place of these four different interests. There was opposition to the appointment of the committee, but it was appointed and met for a year. We had three good Liberals on the board, the late Mr. Spence, Mr. John O'Neill, and another splendid citizen. We went all over the harbours of the world and then made our report, which was adopted; the question was submitted to the people on January 1, 1911, and the by-law was carried by 18,000 to 4,000 odd. The new harbour board made an agreement with the city by which the city government gave to the new harbour board all its property along the waterfront and all the docks at the foot of Yonge and York streets. The dominion government did not give us any property. They then started to improve the western and eastern entrances, and that work has all been completed. A large number of industries have been located in this particular district. Many of the oil and coal companies have located here. The Imperial Oil Company, the British American Oil Company, the McColl Frontenac Oil Company, have spent fortunes in this particular locality. They have built new tankers and are bringing oil and gasoline to Toronto from all over the world. The tonnage in the harbour has increased considerably and this work has all been justified.
After (the people had voted cm. this matter a detailed agreement was drawn up. The minister at that time was Mr. Rogers. The engineers of the dominion government and representatives of the city and the harbour
board met together and an order in council was drawn up upon which was based an act of the parliament of Canada which received the unanimous approval of this house. The commissioners were appointed in 1912; they were Lieutenant-Governor Clark, Mr. Home Smith, Mr. Gourlay, Mr. Spence and myself. I continued in office from 1905 until 1928. I was reappointed at that time but I did not accept the appointment. We received no salary and I know I spent thousands of hours upon1 this work. We would spend as much as two or three days a week and all we received was a lot of (abuse. However, we cleaned up the water front of Toronto and saved1 i:t for the people.
The question of jurisdiction -has come up. The government is committed to the construction of two bridges, one across 'the western channel and one across the eastern channel. We are not abrogating that agreement because it was followed by an act of parliament which was passed in 1913. It was necessary to go to the provincial legislature and to this parliament in order to validate the transfer of the land. The western entrance is a navigable stream and the dominion government has jurisdiction over boundary waterways, over interprovincial streams and over questions affecting navigation. This matter is thus brought within the four comers of .the British North America Act. The same situation arose in- Montreal. I do not object to what was done there; in my opinion that *city was entitled to a large vote for its harbour. As I said this afternoon I believe in the policy of each for all and all for each. The people of Vancouver are just as much interested as we are in a vote for Montreal or Halifax harbours. Waterborne traffic has never had the benefits which have been provided for railibome traffic.
The people who live ton Toronto Island do not own the island. I understand there are only 1,000 leases. Miost of the houses are boarding houses where young people reside during two or three -months in the summer. I should imagine there are about 10,000 residents during -the summer season. The city of Toronto has spent over $100,000 of the taxpayer's money .to improve the island and the revenue does not begin to pay for the expenditures made. It was necessary to extend all services such as gas, electricity, water, telephone, street cleaning and other matters. The island belongs to and is part of the city and is separated from the mainland by the federal entrance. The government has already admitted jurisdiction as it assumes jurisdiction' over the entrances to
Public Works Program

the hanhour. The late government dealt very generously with the city and I want to repeat the tribute I paid them this afternoon. This national scheme for a Toronto harbour was commenced in 1911, 1912 and 1913. The idea was to have it fifty per cent beautification and fifty per cent industrial sites. Industries are locating here to a large extent, so much so that the other day the mayor of Montreal said that they would have to look to their laurels.
An application would have to be made for this tunnel under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, because this channel is a navigable stream just like the St. Lawrence and Ottawa rivers. No erection along, over or under such waters can be made without application under the federal act. This matter will come before the Minister of Public Works in the usual way. Five acres of this harbour property was transferred to Mr. Solman. This was originally a water lot but it had been filled in by the harbour commission and was to be used as a ball park. Last Saturday the board of control passed a resolution strongly in favour of this tunnel. I admit that I was not in favour of this tunnel when I first heard of it some months ago. I thought that we would be abrogating our right to have bridges constructed across the eastern and western entrances. However, I have visited many harbours and I realize that bridges are rapidly being discarded. We have an example in the Detroit river where a traffic tunnel has been built. A tunnel is more economical and efficient and it is possible to have services all the year around.
I am in hopes that this island will be used all the year around and not only for two or three months in the summer time. I want to see the present ramshackle cottages replaced with homes for working people who will be able to get to the island with the payment of one street car fare or possibly an additional one or two cents. This would be much better than having to be put into pig-pens as they are at present or as they were when baseball was being played on the island. I have seen some of my hon. friends across the way at the island in the old days when Toronto had a good team. They will remember the railway crossing at the foot of Bay and Yonge streets and how they had to wait for the ferry boat. They will remember how they did not get home until six or six-thirty o'clock.
At one time a suggestion was made that a bridge be built at the foot of Yonge street to permit passengers to get down to the boats. Like many other projects, this was never gone on with. Instead the city put through the

wider scheme of a viaduct along six miles of the water-front. I believe that Toronto is the only city in Canada which has paid for grade separation. The city of Toronto told the railroads they were ready to do business, they put their cards on the table and to-day there is not a level crossing across the waterfront.
In connection with the use of these lands for an airport, application wild have to be made to the governor in council for permission to divert whatever acreage is necessary for this purpose. As regard the question of jurisdiction, application will have to be made to the minister under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, and he no doubt will see to the insertion in the order in council of the necessary riders to protect navigation. As to the substitution of bridges, the people did not vote on specific bridges; they voted on a wider harbour scheme by which the city, the government and the commission would be required to contribute. So far as the interests of the inhabitants of the island are concerned, that aspect of the matter has been emphasized altogether too much. What about the 650,000 people in the city who pay the taxes to maintain the island? The people on the island get more out of it than anyone else does. Are we not going to consider the interests of these 600,000 or more taxpayers who have to maintain the island, providing various services? I say that the island should belong to all the people all the time and not to some of the people.
I may say that we went into this matter very thoroughly.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Matthews) said that the approaches to this particular tunnel were a matter for the city, but the same principle will have to be adhered to as was observed in connection with the viaduct approaches. As regards the other phases of the matter, an agreement will have to be made between the harbour commission and the city of Toronto, with respect to roads and approaches. I was on the commission for a good many years and if I were asked to undertake the duties again I would not give five minutes of my time to the work, because all that one gets out of it is abuse. When we came here as a harbour commission, however, and represented our case with regard to the viaduct, I must say that we were treated generously by hon. gentlemen opposite, who were the government of that day.

There is one aspect
of this matter that does not seem to have received the attention it deserves, and that is the airport. I do not think there has been

Public Works Program
clearly represented to the house the situation that exists in Toronto in connection with air traffic. It cannot be gainsaid that there is not a city of its size at the present time in North America that has worse air facilities than has Toronto, and the authorities there, realizing that, have had in mind for a number of years some permanent development which would be in keeping with the size and importance of that city. They have been working on the problem. As the former Minister of National Defence said, there was an airdrome at Leaside which was dangerous and has been abandoned. At the present time there are in the north three or four different airdromes but none of them might be called either first class or second class; they have not the facilities to cater to the air trade which offers both from the republic to the south and from the northern country of which Toronto is the logical clearing house. Now the harbour commission fully realized that difficulty and this is not a sudden development which they have proposed; it is one they have been working on for a number of years, the idea being to provide the island with a combined sea and airport which would be suitable for landing seaplanes as well as land machines. When it is fully developed in accordance with the plans that have been laid out, Toronto will have an institution of which it can well be proud, one which will be as efficient as any on the continent. It is very different indeed from the situation in Montreal. Everyone must remember, I think, that this dominion spent over 82,000,000 to equip Montreal with an airport, and of that sum 8500,000 went into the mooring mast for an airship that made only one trip. It was used only on one occasion. That was done by the former government and I find no fault with it at all, but there was an expenditure of $500,000 which, for any use that was made of the structure, might as well have not been made. For that reason it does not seem to me to be out of the way to help Toronto at this time in this particular matter, especially when we remember that there was a dominion commitment of many years' standing with regard to a bridge over that western gap. If we can put a tunnel there instead of the bridge and make possible the development of the airport, I think we shall be doing a very excellent thing. Indeed, I do not know of any one thing that will prove of greater value and more lasting good to Toronto than this combined airport and tunnel, and I think the question should be looked at from that point of view; I do not think that the house should regard it as the outcome of a discussion 92582-185
lasting only a month or two. It is nothing of the kind. It has been carefully thought out and it will be a very useful public work. I know the airport situation there and I submit that it will be of great benefit to the city of Toronto.

My hon. friend has discussed very fairly the provision of airport facilities, but I think he has left a wrong impression on the committee with regard to the airport at St. Hubert. In the first place, Montreal does not enjoy an airport anywhere as close to the city as the airports to the north of the city of Toronto, because St. Hubert is nearly twenty miles from Montreal. In the second place, I think that if the minister looks up the records he will agree with the positive statement I make, that St. Hubert was provided as a national airport to serve as a first-class air base on the eastern coast of the dominion. Aeroplanes contact transatlantic ships, inward or outward, connecting with them at Father Point or even farther down, and it was necessary to have a suitable landing place at a convenient point near the seaboard on the eastern coast of Canada. From here inward overseas mail radiated west and south and to this point was directed mail bound for overseas from a great part of the continent. St. Hubert was not provided as an airport for Montreal and never was so regarded; it was the first great- national airport in Canada. The former government took some care in this matter. The airport was not selected there because it happened to be near Montreal. We had a group of three gentlemen from England, men who understood the requirements of airports and aviation, skilled outstanding men in their profession- one of them was Commander Scott, who perished in the R101, and there were two other gentlemen of outstanding ability-who travelled throughout eastern Canada from Sydney and Halifax to Toronto, examining every possible site in order -to suggest the ideal spot for the purposes of a national port, a terminus for aeroplanes on the eastern coast of Canada. After a most exhaustive examination they unanimously recommended St. Hubert and the Department of National Defence and the government acted on their recommendation. It was in no sense an airport for Montreal. There are a number of sites on the island of Montreal itself which might have been chosen had the interests of the city been the paramount consideration. Those are the circumstances under which St. Hubert was selected.

Public Works Program

With regard to the expenditure on the mooring mast, my hon. friend is quite fair about that; he does not criticize it. The money was voted in order that Canada might do its share in connection with the experimental flight which was proposed to be made by lighter than air craft from England. The Prime Minister of Canada when he was at the imperial conference, in 1928 I think, undertook that if Great Britain would build the ship and send it out, Canada would provide a mooring mast for that purpose. It was as a part in the development of a great commonwealth scheme of aerial transportation that that mooring mast was constructed. My hon. friend was quite right; only one airship landed there-the R100. We all know the very sad tragedy that occurred in connection with lighter than air machines when later the R101 was lost on that fateful trip to India, and since that time Great Britain has not entered extensively into the construction of such machines. It may be that the mooring mast will never be used again. But Canada fulfilled its obligation; it was voted for by every member of this house; there was no opposition to it inside the house. That experiment was conducted safely and successfully I am glad to say, as far as the trip of R100 was concerned, but the R101 met a different fate.
The airport in Toronto is quite a different thing. My hon. friend knows that the policy of the Department of National Defence has been that airports are to be established by municipal authorities. Assistance by the Department of National Defence and the government of Canada is given in the way of lighting them and providing accessories. But the airport itself, as far as I know, and I do not think my hon. friend has made any change in that regard, has been provided by the municipality. While my hon. friend has made a contribution to this debate in suggesting that airport facilities at Toronto are not as good as they should be, I do not think he has advanced any argument why we should spend a million dollars, not for an airport but for a tunnel without any suggestion of any commitment by anyone to construct an airport in Toronto at the terminus of this tunnel. We come back to that time and time again no matter how much we may appear to wander from it; the vote now is for a tunnel from the city of Toronto to an island in Toronto harbour. One of the members for Toronto who just sat down gave the thing pretty well away, I think, when he suggested that one argument in favour of this thing is that if that tunnel were built residents of

Toronto could ride to the island for the price of a street car fare. What has that to do with the dominion government, with dominion funds? No matter how deserving the people may be, is this house going to vote special funds to provide them with cheap transportation facilities? Are we going to vote funds to reduce the city transportation fares of Winnipeg, of Calgary, or of Vancouver? The argument is just as strong for on-e place as the other. I think the hon. member brought out very forcibly the point we are trying to make, namely that so far as any evidence submitted to this committee goes, this tunnel is not a national project, it is purely a local project; in connection with the national aspect of it there has been no commitment or definite assurance whatever, and I submit that as a project in conjunction with an airport which may or may not materialize, it is a project which requires, as the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott) says, a good deal more examination and careful study and investigation and reports from competent aviation engineers than appear to have 'been given or supplied having regard to the meagre information that has been laid before this committee.

speechtext:
I am very glad we agree
on that point. The argument I was going to make was this. After looking over the schedule as a whole, at first sight it would appear that as the government was spending money in the harbour of Montreal and the harbour of Quebec it was also desired to spend money in the harbour of Toronto, but the moment we examine into the matter more closely we find that this tunnel project as an improvement to the harbour of Toronto simply does not exist. It cannot improve the harbour of Toronto at all.
The argument that is advanced in favour of this project is twofold. In the first place, it is said that an agreement was entered into with the city of Toronto some twenty-five years ago, as the minister has just repeated. In the second place, it is said that this tunnel might serve as an access to an airport which does not yet exist. I say that in both cases the argument is a very poor one.
In the first place, if the agreement has been left outstanding for a great number of years, no attempt being made to carry it out even when the country was prosperous and a lot of money could be spent everywhere, it is disputable at this stage, when money even for relief purposes is very cautiously spent, whether the agreement entered into some twenty-five years ago should be respected when it is acknowledged to-night that this tunnel is of no use at all so far as an improvement to the harbour is concerned. In the second place, we are told that the tunnel will furnish access to an airport. Certainly, Mr. Chairman, this is the first time that we hear of building an expensive access to something that does not exist. It would be much wiser first to let the airport be built, and then consider whether it would be worth while to have such an expensive method of access constructed.
Another argument which in my opinion is a very poor one is that this project is for relief purposes and to provide employment. That argument could be advanced in favour of anything at all proposed under this act. Of course we want money to be spent to relieve unemployment, but the mere fact that
it is to be spent for that purpose is no reason why we should build a tunnel rather than a bridge, or this work rather than another. I find that under item No. 10. for instance, there is a large amount appropriated without any specific purpose being set forth, and the proposal that has been made by my hon. friend from Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor) I think is a good one, that instead of having this one million dollars voted specifically for a tunnel it might be included in the general vote with the understanding that Toronto will have the benefit of it. If it is not used for a tunnel it might be used for a public building or improvements of another kind, and that would be serving the purpose of providing employment, for which we all stand. But it is not necessary to have the money voted specifically for a tunnel.
The minister seems to think we must take the bill as it stands, that we cannot possibly change one line of it. But this would surely be the first piece of legislation to come before the house. Mr. Chairman, in respect to which it was not considered possible to bring in any amendment. Surely the minister will not say it would not be feasible to withdraw that one line appropriating a million dollars for a tunnel at the west entrance of Toronto harbour and to add one million dollars to the amount appropriated in item No. 10. On the contrary. I think it would be very wise and very reasonable. Then it would be understood that one million dollars would be spent in Toronto anyway for the relief of unemployment, but we would not be committing ourselves to the building of a tunnel which in the words of the minister himself is not an improvement to the harbour but will lead to an airport which does not exist, and is being imposed upon a city which does not want it.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT

I have the floor, Mr. Chairman; I am trying to use it as a gentleman and my hon. friend will not interrupt me unless he does likewise. We have heard a good deal about the airdrome at St. Hubert in connection writh Montreal harbour, and when I said that this proposed tunnel would not be an improvement to the harbour of Toronto the minister would not even let me finish my sentence. This tunnel is proposed merely because it was agreed some twenty-five years ago that there might be built either a tunnel or a bridge, and there is the additional argument that it would lead to an airport when nobody knows whether the airport will ever be constructed. You do not need to be from Toronto to understand that the whole thing is absurd. It is very clear to a member coming from any part of Canada; and I will never admit in this house-I say this dispassionately

that unless you happen to reside in the very place where an expenditure is proposed you have no right to discuss it. If my hon. friend from Parkdale has that parochial idea, I have not. I claim the right to discuss expenditures in Halifax and Vancouver with the same dispassionate freedom that I have when it comes to discussing an expenditure in my own city. But I will not prolong that part of the argument. I know that my hon. friend (Mr. Spence) is very genial. He just popped up at the moment and regrets it I am sure, and I accept his apology even before he presents it to me.

It might be permissible
to point out that the discussion to-day has brought out the fact that the federal government contemplates the expenditure of $1,000,000 to build a tunnel to connect the city of Toronto with an island in Toronto harbour, towards which the city of Toronto is to make a contribution of something like $100,000. This is not a necessary work. The minister has indicated that this work is being undertaken with a view to providing work for the unemployed, but I would point out that the city of Winnipeg is in a dire and desperate condition due to the necessity for sewage disposal. This work will cost some $900,000 and the federal authorities are offering assistance only to the extent of forty per cent. It is almost impossible to live along the banks of the Red river in the summer time because of the stench caused by insufficient water to carry away the sewage. speechtext:
I practised in Toronto for many years and I have been in St. John's ward many times. Lieutenant-Governor Bruce brought in a report on slum conditions and I feel sure that the vast majority of the people of Toronto would rather clean up the slums and provide proper homes for these people than build this tunnel. Parts of these slums are in close contact with the better parts of the city. I agree with the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor) who suggests that this money be set aside and not allocated to any particular purpose until such time as we hear from the people of Toronto. If the people desire to spend this money on a housing scheme it would be much better than building a tunnel. With a housing scheme there would be some return from the money invested, besides providing comfort for the people. Under this bill it is proposed to build a tunnel which is not necessary.
It also is suggested that an airdrome is to be constructed on a seventy-five acre lot. There does not seem to be any more acreage and I cannot imagine how an airdrome which usually requires some three or four hundred acres can be built on a lot that size. It is suggested that seventy-five per cent of this expenditure will be used for labour, but I would direct the attention of the committee to the fact that this labour will be mostly pick and shovel labour. If a housing scheme was undertaken employment would be provided for bricklayers, plasterers, caipenters and other forms of labour. Under this proposal a large percentage of the money will go to the big contractors, because much of the work will be done by machinery. The housing scheme, in my opinion, would be much better because it would give work to the unemployed in Toronto. This is a matter that should be referred back to the city of Toronto and I am sure that we might very well act on their advice. We might ask them how they would wish to spend the money to provide relief for the unemployed. If it were spent in connection with a housing scheme it would save the country north of Toronto from the travellers who are a public nuisance on the highways. I would gladly vote for a scheme that would keep the people of Toronto occupied so as to get them off our highways. It would also relieve the hon. member for Parkdale because he would not then find it necessary to provide a lot of ribbons and buttons for people at the next election. At the last election men were wearing buttons on
Public Works Program

their coats and they were all unemployed. I moved from one place to another and asked these men what they had been doing in the afternoon-this procession took place after six o'clock-and I found that about one-third of them had been working. speechtext:
There is one phase of
this matter that has not been fairly stated. I have elicited from the minister the fact that practically $9,000,000 has been expended by the federal government in connection with the work in that harbour since the agreement was entered into. I happen to know something about the way in which these expenditures were made. They were made as a fulfilment in part of promises contained in that agreement. The agreement has not been placed before the committee, but the minister has given a memorandum containing some of the things set forth in it. The agreement was not an undertaking to do within any definite time all these works included in it; the work was to be done when funds were available, or words to that effect. It was never contemplated that this government should be called upon to make an expenditure of that kind as a matter of obligation under the agreement in times like these. That a bascule bridge, estimated originally to cost $800,000. was not built was due largely to the

fact that after a time there crept into the minds of the harbour commissioners a doubt as to whether such a bridge was desirable at that point.
Progress reported.

inform the house that I have received the resignation of Alfred Burke Thompson, Esquire, as member for the electoral district of East Simcoe.
